passages.where: Jesus tells this story to Pharisees and scribes who grumble that he welcomes sinners (Luke 15:1-2). The father sees his son while he is still far off and runs to him before the son can finish the speech he rehearsed.

The same father goes out a second time, now to the older son who stayed home and stands angry outside the feast. Both sons were far from him in their own way, and the story ends without saying whether the older one goes in.
The first of the three stories Jesus tells the grumblers. The shepherd does not wait for the lost sheep to find its own way back; he goes after it until he finds it.

God speaks of Israel as a son he loved, called out of Egypt and taught to walk, who ran from him toward other gods the more he called. Judgment is coming, and still God's own heart recoils from giving his child up. Scripture's own picture of God includes a parent with a wayward child.

King David hears that his son Absalom, who had raised an army against him, is dead. Absalom's rebellion was real and it was his own. David's grief is still a father's grief, and the Bible sets it down without tidying it into a lesson.

The exiles in Babylon were repeating a proverb that blamed their suffering on their parents' sins. God forbids it: each person answers to him for his own ways. It cuts both ways for a parent. You cannot carry your child's choices for them, and their choices are not simply a verdict on you.

Zion, the people in exile, complains that the LORD has forgotten her. God answers with the strongest bond anyone knew, a mother and her nursing child, and says his own love holds even where that bond could fail.

Luke gives the point before the story: pray at all times and do not lose heart. A widow keeps coming to a judge who cares for no one. The story works by contrast. God is not that judge; he hears his people day and night.

James ends his letter by asking believers to bring back anyone who wanders from the truth. It takes for granted that wandering happens inside the church, and that bringing someone back is ordinary Christian work, often done by someone other than a parent.

Peter answers scoffers who say Christ's promised coming will never arrive. The delay is not slowness but patience: God wants people to come to repentance. The patience is God's before it is ever a parent's.

misread.taken: Many parents have been told this verse is a promise: raise a child the right way and he will come back. When a child does not come back, the same verse turns into an accusation, sometimes from other people and more often from the parent's own heart.
misread.says: Proverbs is a book of sayings about how life usually goes. This one is true and encouraging: early training tends to shape a whole life. It is not a contract. The same book keeps warning sons who were taught well not to leave what they were taught (Proverbs 19:27), and the Bible tells of good parents with wayward children and of bad parents with faithful ones. Interpreters also differ on what “the way he should go” means. On any reading the verse asks parents to take the task seriously. It does not make a parent the only cause of a child's faith or unbelief, and it gives no one leave to blame a grieving parent.

whole: A child's wandering rarely arrives as one event. It comes as a skipped Sunday, then a silence at the table, then a conversation that ends with a door closing. Parents who love God often carry it in two layers at once: the grief of watching a child walk away, and the private fear that it is their fault. The second layer is often the heavier one, because it can be carried in secret and it never stops asking questions.

The Bible does not hide this grief. It tells it in its first families and keeps on telling it: Cain, the sons of Eli, the sons of Jacob who sold their brother, David and Absalom. And it tells it of God. Through Hosea, God speaks of Israel as a child he taught to walk, who went further away the more he called. The wayward child is not a modern problem, and it is not proof that one family was unusually careless. It is one of the oldest stories in Scripture, and God puts himself inside it as the parent.

Two things follow, and each needs the other. The first is that a child is a person before God, not the product of a method. Ezekiel 18 will not let one generation blame the last, and it will not let parents carry their children's choices as if they had made them. A parent can own real failures, and most will find some, without taking on the whole weight of a choice that belonged to someone else.

The second is that hope here is not wishful thinking. The father in Luke 15 does not chase his son into the far country, and he does not pretend the son never left. He keeps watching the road, and when the son comes he runs. Then he goes out again, to the son who never left but was just as far from him. Christian hope for a wandering child rests on that kind of God: one who goes after the lost, whose patience is longer than ours, and who can reach a child in places a parent never will. The waiting can be long, and not every story ends the way a parent prays it will. But a parent waits as someone who is also loved, not as someone on trial.

differ.share: All Christians hold that salvation is God's work, that praying for a child who has wandered is right, and that only God knows how a person's story ends.

views.name: Kept to the end
views.body: Many Reformed and Baptist churches teach that those whom God truly saves are kept by him to the end. A child who once professed faith and has walked away may yet return, or may not have known Christ as the parent hoped. Parents in these churches pray for God to do what only he can do.

views.name: Faith that can be lost
views.body: Wesleyan, Methodist and many Pentecostal churches, and the Catholic and Orthodox churches in their own terms, teach that a real believer can turn away from Christ and be lost. Parents in these churches pray for a child to come back to a faith that was real.

differ.after: Both pray the same prayer and hand the child to the same God. The Honest Answer “Can you lose your salvation?” sets out the question at more length.

sit: What would change in how you speak to your child this month if you believed their story was not over, and that you are not its author?

prayer.lead: Psalm 130 was prayed by someone still waiting when it ended. Pray it slowly, and put your child's name where the psalm says Israel.
